newsitem.title: UK: UK economy swings government's way as election nears.
newsitem.headline: UK economy swings government's way as election nears.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives have long been hoping that economic recovery would rescue them from disaster at the looming general election.
With no more than eight months until polling day, there are signs that the final pieces of the economic jigsaw may be starting to slip into place.

Consumers are spending more, unemployment is falling, interest rates are at 30-year lows and house prices are picking up. Manufacturing, until now the weak link in the recovery, is finally emerging from the doldrums.

Inflation, unusually low by historical standards, is proving a touch recalcitrant, hovering just above the government target. But the trend is favourable and even the hawkish Bank of England accepts that it will fall in the next few months.

Although the opposition Labour party still has a strong lead in opinion polls, the Conservatives have begun narrowing the gap and many City economists believe they will continue to gain ground as the election, due by next May, approaches.
"The question is if this will make the difference between a Conservative majority and some other outcome," says Ian Stewart, an economist at Merrill Lynch.
Stewart says the "misery index" -- an informal measure made up of interest rates, inflation and unemployment rates -- is at a 20-year low and should fall further.
The bank calculates its own "well-being index," which Stewart says has predicted Conservative support fairly accurately over the last 16 years.
"On the basis of this experience we are looking for a big bounce in Conservative support in the published opinion polls between now and the election," he says.
Anthony King, a polling expert at Essex University, says the "feelgood factor" is coming right for the government, but only very gradually.

"The government is still given little credit for its handling of the economy," he wrote in the Daily Telegraph newspaper. "The Tories are gradually eroding Labour's lead...but the process is so far proving glacial."
A welcome crumb of comfort for the government came in an August MORI poll showing the Conservatives had narrowly overtaken Labour as the party most trusted to run the economy.
Reponsibility for translating economic recovery into Conservative votes rests squarely on Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke.

He needs to deploy the twin weapons in his armoury -- taxes and interest rates -- to ensure the government reaps maximum credit while avoiding charges that it is manipulating the economy for overtly political purposes.
Many economists believe Clarke may have used all his ammunition as far as monetary policy is concerned.
He has cut official interest rates four times since December to their present 5.75 percent level, giving millions of home-owners the cheapest home loans for a generation.
But his last rate cut in June incurred the wrath of the Bank of England, which fears inflationary pressures may be building up in the future and opposes any further easing.
A slight pickup in manufacturing and the stubborn refusal of underlying inflation to dip below 2.8 percent in the past four months have weakened the economic case for another cut.
"The economy is moving ahead now under its own steam," says Tom Rayner, an economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.
"Another rate cut at this stage would just risk the inflation target and is not necessary to ensure that the economy recovers throughout next year."

Clarke's dilemma is that if he decides to leave interest rates where they are and the Conservatives lose the election, he could be made a scapegoat and forfeit any chances he may have of one day becoming party leader.

A politically suspect rate cut, on the other hand, could undermine sterling and put upward pressure on interest rates in the government bond market, possibly forcing Clarke to raise rates again within months.
The safer option therefore may be for the Chancellor to concentrate his fire on the November 26 budget.

A cut in the basic rate of income tax to 23 percent from 24 percent is seen as a virtual certainty, with the lost revenue clawed back through spending cuts to ensure the budget deficit does not increase.

This would have the twin attraction for the government of showing up in workers' pay packets next April, a month before the likely election date, while possibly embarrassing Labour, which is working hard to persuade voters that it would not increase taxes.
While the economy may be going the government's way at the moment, there is no guarantee that progress will be uninterrupted or that it will be enough to swing the election towards the Conservatives.
"The most likely result of a Tory comeback in the polls is not victory but a hung parliament or a small Labour majority," Stewart said.
Douglas McWilliams of the Centre for Economics and Business (CEBR) Research agrees.

"As the election approaches, the 'feelgood factor' will start to be eroded by uncertainty as the electorate start to suspect that their tax cuts will be taken away from them," he wrote in the latest CEBR economic report.

"The most likely result would be either a Labour win with a small majority or a hung parliament, with smaller parties voting against a continuation of Conservative rule. But politics is even more uncertain than economics and there is still a 25 percent chance of the Conservatives being returned with a majority."
